children.text: Cavitation

A spherical bubble in infinite, homogeneous, inviscid, incompressible water contains vapour and possibly air. Neglect gravity, translation and air migration except where a question explicitly includes them. Vapour pressure remains at \(p_v\) through rapid evaporation and condensation, and water temperature is constant. Bubble radius is R, far-field pressure \(p_\infty\), water density \(\rho=997\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), surface tension \(\sigma=72.8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N/m}\), and \(p_v=2340\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Unless stated otherwise \(p_\infty=101\,\mathrm{kPa}\). Air is ideal with adiabatic exponent \(\gamma=1.4\), reference partial pressure q0 at radius R0, and atmospheric density \(\delta=1.29\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\). For dissolved air, Henry law is \(u=Hq\), \(H=0.24\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^2/m^2}\). Diffusivity is \(\kappa=2\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}\), with outward flux \(-\kappa\partial u/\partial r\). The supplied half-line heat-equation kernel is \([e^{-(x-y)^2/(4t)}-e^{-(x+y)^2/(4t)}]/\sqrt{4\pi t}\). Useful integrals are \(\int_0^\infty e^{-bx^2}dx=\sqrt\pi/(2\sqrt b)\) and \(\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-bx^2}dx=\sqrt\pi/(4b^{3/2})\). Several numerical values in the retained solution use different constants from the statement. Use the statement constants here.

children.text: A.1. Collapse time scale
Estimate the collapse time of a pure-vapour bubble with R0=1 mm, no surface tension, and the stated pressures. Set the dimensionless factor to one.
A.2. Critical pressure
A bubble with \(R_0=10^{-5}\,\mathrm m\) starts in equilibrium at 101 kPa. Find q0, then lower pressure gradually with isothermal air. Find the critical external pressure for unbounded growth.
B.1. Bubble equation of motion
Derive the radius equation and insert adiabatic air pressure.
B.2. Exposure to vacuum
A 10 micrometre nucleus initially in equilibrium at 101 kPa is suddenly exposed to vacuum. Estimate its asymptotic growth speed and the time scale to reach that regime.
B.3. Pressure-jump rebound
A 10 micrometre gas bubble starts in equilibrium at \(p^-_\infty=1600\,\mathrm{Pa}\), then the far pressure jumps to 101 kPa. Estimate minimum radius before rebound.
B.4. Final-collapse exponent
For pure vapour with complete collapse at time T, find alpha in \(R\sim(T-t)^\alpha\).
B.5. Bubble resonance
Find the natural radial frequency of an equilibrium bubble of radius R0=0.1 mm.
B.6. Standing-wave force
A small bubble at x=0 is driven by \(p=p_0+A\sin[k(x+a)]\sin\omega t\), \(\omega=2\pi f,k=\omega/c\). Find the mean force, treating the small response linearly away from resonance.
C.1. Diffusive dissolution

A nucleus with R0=10 micrometres and air pressure \(q=1.70\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) lies in water saturated with air at atmospheric pressure. Neglect vapour. Estimate dissolution time, assuming diffusion extends much farther than the bubble radius.

children.text: Cavitation
A.1. Collapse time scale
Dimensional analysis using the positive driving pressure gives \[T\sim R_0\sqrt{\rho/(p_\infty-p_v)}=1.01\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm s.\] The retained solution prints 0.1 s, a factor of 1000 too large.
A.2. Critical pressure

Laplace balance gives \(q_0=p_\infty-p_v+2\sigma/R_0=113220\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Isothermal conservation gives \(q=q_0R_0^3/R^3\), hence \(p_\infty(R)=p_v+q_0R_0^3/R^3-2\sigma/R\). Its minimum occurs at \(R_c=\sqrt{3q_0R_0^3/(2\sigma)}=48.3\,\mu\mathrm m\). Therefore \(p_c=p_v-4\sigma/(3R_c)\simeq331\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The published q0 and threshold use different surface-tension data.
B.1. Bubble equation of motion

Incompressibility gives radial water speed \(v(r,t)=R^2\dot R/r^2\). Integrate the radial Euler equation from R to infinity and add the Laplace jump. The Rayleigh-Plesset equation without viscosity is \[\rho(R\ddot R+\tfrac32\dot R^2)=p_v+q_0(R_0/R)^{3\gamma}-p_\infty-2\sigma/R.\] The vapour term stays constant while the air term changes adiabatically.
B.2. Exposure to vacuum

The formal large-radius limit is \(\dot R_\infty=\sqrt{2p_v/(3\rho)}=1.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\), but one must first check whether the initial bubble can reach that branch. With the adiabatic air law from B.1, \(q_0=113220\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and \(x=R/R_0\), integration of the radius equation gives \[\dot R^2=\frac2\rho\left[\frac{p_v}{3}(1-x^{-3})+\frac{q_0}{3(1-\gamma)}(x^{-3\gamma}-x^{-3})-\frac\sigma{R_0}(x^{-1}-x^{-3})\right].\] The right-hand side first returns to zero at \(x=5.26846\), after about \(7.06\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\). The bubble therefore reaches about 52.7 micrometres and rebounds. It cannot cross the negative-square-speed interval to the formal unbounded branch. Thus the stated adiabatic model has no accessible terminal growth speed or settling time for these initial data. If the air is instead kept isothermal, the critical pressure from A.2 is positive, vacuum lies below it and unbounded expansion is possible. Its formal limiting speed is then 1.25 m/s. The source's initial estimate \(\dot R_\infty/\ddot R(0)\simeq1.2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm s\) is not a settling time, even in that alternative model. State the thermal assumption and compare both interpretations. This part requires self-review.
B.3. Pressure-jump rebound

Initial balance gives \(q_0=1600-2340+14560=13820\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Multiply the motion equation by \(R^2\dot R\) and integrate. At a turning point, with \(x=R/R_0\), \[0=\frac{p_\infty-p_v}{3}(x^3-1)+\frac\sigma{R_0}(x^2-1)+\frac{q_0}{3(\gamma-1)}(x^{3-3\gamma}-1).\] Select the smaller positive root, excluding initial x=1. It gives a radius of about 3 micrometres. The source estimate 0.4 micrometres uses a much smaller q0 that is inconsistent with the statement. The source small-radius asymptotic formula is not reliable at the corrected moderate compression.
B.4. Final-collapse exponent
The dominant inward kinetic-energy balance gives \(\dot R\sim-R^{-3/2}\). Integrating yields \(R^{5/2}\propto T-t\), so \(\alpha=2/5\).
B.5. Bubble resonance

Linearize with \(R=R_0(1+y)\): \[\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=0,\quad\omega_0^2=\frac{3\gamma q_0-2\sigma/R_0}{\rho R_0^2},\quad q_0=p_\infty-p_v+2\sigma/R_0.\] Hence \(f_0=\omega_0/(2\pi)\simeq32.6\,\mathrm{kHz}\).
B.6. Standing-wave force

The external pressure drives \(\rho R_0^2(\ddot y+\omega_0^2y)=-A\sin(ka)\sin\omega t\). Thus \(y=-A\sin(ka)\sin\omega t/[\rho R_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)]\). Average \(F_x=-\langle V\partial_xp\rangle\) with \(V\simeq4\pi R_0^3(1+3y)/3\): \[\langle F_x\rangle=\frac{\pi R_0A^2k\sin(2ka)}{\rho(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}=\frac{fA^2R_0\sin(4\pi fa/c)}{2\rho c(f_0^2-f^2)}.\] Below resonance bubbles are driven towards pressure antinodes. The retained solution loses the minus sign in the pressure forcing and consequently reverses the force. At resonance the undamped steady linear formula fails.
C.1. Diffusive dissolution

The spherical diffusion equation is \(u_t=\kappa(u_{rr}+2u_r/r)\). The quasi-steady profile gives outward air loss \(dm/dt=-4\pi\kappa RH(q-p_\infty)\). Mechanical equilibrium requires \(q=p_\infty+2\sigma/R\). With \(m=(4\pi/3)\delta(q/p_\infty)R^3\) and \(\epsilon=2\sigma\delta/p_\infty\), integration gives \[T=\frac{\delta R_0^3+\epsilon R_0^2}{6\sigma\kappa H}\simeq7\,\mathrm s.\] Direct integration of \(\delta R^2+(2/3)\epsilon R\) produces epsilon with coefficient one, not four as printed in the retained solution. The stated q=170 kPa is also not in mechanical equilibrium at R0 with the other given constants, which instead imply 115.56 kPa. Using a fixed prescribed q throughout gives a different approximate diffusion-only model. The self-consistent equilibrium estimate above explains this limitation rather than imposing a unique numerical key.
C.2. Air trapped in a crevice

The interface obeys \(p_v+q=p_\infty\pm2\sigma/R\) with curvature sign chosen from the geometry, and \(u=Hq\). A curvature that opposes diffusive squeezing allows a stable trapped pocket. With the source contact-angle convention its geometric condition is \(2\theta>\pi+\alpha\). The angle convention and curvature orientation are essential.
